title: Multi-Rail Cash-Flow Underwriting After UPI Fees
one_liner: When UPI stops being free for big tickets, reconstruct small-merchant revenue from GST, bank and supplier data instead of UPI alone.
customer: NBFCs, small finance banks and cash-flow lenders that lend to kirana and small retail businesses.
problem: Lenders assumed UPI data was the universal truth for underwriting. The Oct 15 MDR (0.4% above Rs 2,000, capped at Rs 300) hits about 4% of P2M volume but about 66% of value, so merchants now have a reason to route big tickets through cash or bank transfer.
solution: An API that combines Account Aggregator bank data, GST e-invoice and filing data, supplier invoices and soundbox/QR data into a revenue estimate with a rail-shift adjustment. The wedge is a turnover sanity-check score for five NBFCs.
why_now: MDR starts Oct 15, the Supreme Court refused a stay, and retailers are organising protests. RBI's cash-flow lending push depends on this data.
revenue_model: Rs 40-120 per scored application plus a monitoring fee on the live loan book.
non_obvious_insight: A fee on exactly the high-value 66% creates an incentive to hide it. The rail shift is a data-quality shock, and the first lender to model it gets an underwriting edge.
first_30_days: Get consented data on about 200 existing borrowers from one NBFC partner and backtest against repayments. Offer a 60-day free pilot.

title: Nonrenewal Cure: Rebutting Insurer Cancellations
one_liner: Nonrenewal notices often cite fixable issues like roof condition, tree overhang or debris. Sell homeowners a fast diagnosis, repair and evidence packet to get re-underwritten instead of dumped on a FAIR plan.
customer: Homeowners in CA, FL, TX, CO, UT and NM who have received a nonrenewal notice, plus independent brokers who lose those clients.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and homeowners have 30-75 days to react. Carriers are structurally conflicted about helping, and the FAIR plan is pricey with thin cover. Homeowners can't decode the reason code, can't tell which items are cheap to fix, and can't produce the evidence a carrier re-inspection accepts.
solution: Upload the notice. The service decodes the stated reason using state disclosure rules, dispatches vetted local contractors for the fix (patch, trim, vent screens), and produces a time-stamped photo and invoice packet. It files for reinspection or appeal, and gives the broker a clean file to re-market the risk. For wildfire-score cases it documents mitigation credits available under state rules.
why_now: Record nonrenewals, California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03, and insurance now rivals mortgage payments. Carriers rely more on aerial-imagery flags that homeowners rarely see or contest.
revenue_model: $149 diagnostic, $250-$500 evidence packet, 10-15% contractor referral fee, and broker referral fees on re-placed policies.
non_obvious_insight: Many cancellations are cheap to cure, but the homeowner has no language, time or evidence, and the carrier won't help. A homeowner who has just been rescued becomes a lifetime referral source for brokers.
first_30_days: Post in local nonrenewal threads and neighborhood groups, and partner with three independent brokers. Handle 20 cases by hand, track how many carriers reinstate, and use the win rate to set pricing.

title: Copyright-Registration Autopilot for AI Settlements
one_liner: Monthly bulk US copyright registration and an evidence vault for creators, so they are eligible when AI settlements and claims open.
customer: Newsletter writers, podcasters, photographers, illustrators and indie musicians, plus small publishers and labels, most of whom have never registered a work.
problem: In the Anthropic authors settlement (Sep 2025), only works with timely US registrations qualified, and new music and news suits (for example UMG and Sony against Suno, per the brief) follow the same logic. Registration also gates suing at all and statutory damages. Most independent creators skip it because of fees and friction, which puts them at the back of every claims line.
solution: OAuth into Substack, Beehiiv, Ghost, Bandcamp and portfolio storage. The service assembles the right group registrations (short online literary works, photographs, unpublished works, albums), files them with the Copyright Office, tracks registration numbers and deposit copies, and keeps a tamper-evident vault of first-publication evidence. A claims desk alerts users when a settlement or class definition matches their registered works. Has an attorney review the workflow.
why_now: The 2025-2026 AI settlements and suits made registration status the gating asset. Creator demand for anything that pays them from AI is high, and the Suno-Warner settlement shows deals are landing.
revenue_model: $19-39/month plus pass-through Copyright Office fees, a $99 first-year catch-up batch, and an optional 10% of recovered settlement payouts through the claims desk.
non_obvious_insight: Class-action money goes to the paperwork-ready. For an AI-era creator, registration status may be the most valuable and most neglected asset, and the boring gate is where a subscription business sits.
first_30_days: Partner with a copyright attorney to design the workflow. Pilot with 50 newsletter writers and 20 illustrators from creator communities, using a free 'AI-claims readiness audit' as the lead magnet.

title: Launch Kits for the First Psilocybin Clinics
one_liner: A readiness and operations service that helps ketamine and TMS clinics and state-licensed psilocybin centers get staffed, compliant and billable before the first FDA approval.
customer: Interventional psychiatry clinics (ketamine, TMS, Spravato sites) and state-licensed psilocybin service centers in Oregon and Colorado, paying $8-20k for a readiness audit plus $3-6k a month for ops software.
problem: Trend chain: Compass's COMP360 has positive phase 3 data and a new CEO (Sep 2026) for a 'coming launch', so an approval is plausible within about a year (timing uncertain). Then treatment needs 6-8 hour monitored dosing sessions with trained monitors, recovery rooms, screening, integration follow-up and prior authorization. Then the sites have four times the chair-time of Spravato, no proven billing model, and some Oregon centers have already closed for lack of economics.
solution: Phase 1: a readiness audit covering space design, staffing model, screening protocol, day-long-session P&L, and payer mix, plus monitor training through partners. Phase 2: ops software for scheduling day-long sessions, pooling monitors across clinics, integration follow-up, REMS-style reporting and prior-auth packets.
why_now: Compass is preparing filing and launch. Oregon's program is live and Colorado opened licensed healing centers in 2025, so a paying pilot audience exists today. The 2024 FDA rejection of Lykos's MDMA showed how much process rigor matters. Ketamine clinics are consolidating and want a new line.
revenue_model: Readiness audit fee, monthly ops subscription, training seat fees, and a margin on a shared monitor staffing pool.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck for the first psychedelic drug is chair-hours, not efficacy: 6-8 staffed hours per treatment with no settled reimbursement. The team that builds the day-long-session P&L and staffing model first owns the picks-and-shovels position.
first_30_days: Interview 20 ketamine and TMS clinic owners and 5 Oregon or Colorado center owners. Publish a free 'psilocybin chair-hour P&L calculator' to capture leads. Sell three readiness audits at $8-10k.

title: Josephine Reborn: Permit Concierge for Home Kitchens
one_liner: Josephine's home-cooked-meal marketplace was boxed in by health law; California's MEHKO law now licenses home restaurants, so build the permit concierge and a compliant direct-to-consumer storefront, not another marketplace.
customer: Home cooks, especially immigrant and regional-cuisine specialists (tamales, Armenian, Korean, Oaxacan, Filipino), in Los Angeles County and the roughly 19 California jurisdictions that had authorized MEHKOs as of May 2026. Many already sell via Instagram and WhatsApp without a permit.
problem: MEHKO caps are 30 meals/day, 90/week and roughly $107k/year. Applying costs about $597 plus about $347/yr in LA County, plus food-handler certification, menu SOPs, labels, sales logs and inspections. Third-party delivery apps are restricted, so cooks cannot just list on DoorDash. No tool enforces the caps, produces inspector-ready records, or helps neighbors find them, and paperwork is mostly in English.
solution: A permit concierge ($249-399 one-time) that completes the application, SOPs and multilingual allergen labels. Then a $20/mo cook operating system: link-in-bio storefront with pre-orders and pickup windows, automatic sell-out at 30/day and 90/week, temperature and sales logs exported in the county's format, and Stripe payments. Demand comes from neighborhood 'Friday drop' maps and newsletters and workplace pickup clusters. Cooks own their customers; there is no marketplace.
why_now: MEHKO adoption is spreading county by county (17 counties plus Berkeley and Long Beach by May 2026), with LA County running an active program. Restaurant prices are high, social commerce is normal, and AI makes multilingual SOPs and labels nearly free. A few early MEHKO startups exist, so the opening is to be permit-first, multilingual and neighborhood-by-neighborhood.
revenue_model: $249-399 permit concierge fee; $20/mo per cook SaaS; roughly 1% payments margin; affiliate income from food-handler training and liability insurance. Later, a bulk-permitting contract with counties that want cleaner inspection records.
non_obvious_insight: The marketplace was the illegal or unscalable part, and under MEHKO it is structurally limited to direct-to-consumer sales. The scarce asset is the permit, and the winning product is compliance and storefront tooling that turns each cook into her own licensed restaurant. Enforcing the meal caps in software becomes a feature, and it makes the vendor the county health department's preferred partner.
first_30_days: Attend LA County MEHKO office hours. Find 10 cooks on Instagram (#lahomecook, #tamales) and do their applications free in exchange for case studies. Build the storefront with Shopify or Stripe plus a no-code cap rule. Target 5 issued permits within about 60 days, then start charging the $20/mo.

title: Cap Ledger for the 350-Home Rule
one_liner: An ownership graph that counts which LLCs a single-family rental owner controls, proves grandfathering and build-to-rent exemption, and becomes the audit trail lenders and buyers demand.
customer: SFR operators and funds with 100-2,000 homes (the almost-institutional tier), their lenders and securitization arrangers, and M&A counsel doing diligence.
problem: The ROAD to Housing Act caps institutional single-family-rental owners at 350 homes, exempts build-to-rent and grandfathers existing owners, but leaves key definitions and reporting mechanics unspecified. Owners hold homes through hundreds of LLCs and JVs, and nobody can currently prove a per-owner count, per-home acquisition date or build-to-rent status.
solution: Build a parcel-level ownership graph from county deeds, mailing addresses, secretary-of-state filings and mortgage records. Output each owner's 'cap position' plus a per-home evidence file (acquisition date, certificate-of-occupancy and first-lease date for BTR). A rules engine updates as regulations finalize, plus a 'what if I buy 60 more homes' scenario tool.
why_now: The cap and grandfathering are new, definitions are ambiguous, and every operator, lender and buyer suddenly needs a defensible number. Whoever's ledger regulators and counterparties adopt sets the standard.
revenue_model: $1-3 per home per year SaaS, $5-15K diligence packages per transaction, and lender portfolio-monitoring licenses.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders read the cap as a threat to institutional SFR, but a cap on new purchases makes grandfathered portfolios scarce capacity and makes provable status a balance-sheet asset. The graph also reveals 'independent' operators that are secretly affiliated, which is valuable to both sides. Sell the ledger, not a fixed reading of rules that will move.
first_30_days: Build the graph for two metros (for example Atlanta and Phoenix) from public deed data. Rank the top 50 owners and cold-email operators in the 100-1,000 home band with their own cap-position PDF. Convert 3 into $10K design-partner pilots. Retain an attorney to track rulemaking.

title: Chaos Testing for Buildings as Code-Required Commissioning
one_liner: An agent that safely actuates a building's HVAC at night, forcing dampers, valves and pumps through scripted step tests, to produce the functional-test evidence that codes require and passive analytics cannot.
customer: Commissioning firms and energy-service companies, and owners of 100k-2M sq ft commercial buildings facing performance standards (NYC Local Law 97, Washington and Denver building performance standards) and California Title 24 acceptance testing.
problem: Passive fault-detection analytics cannot tell 'stuck damper' from 'no demand'. Functional performance tests are still done by hand on clipboards at handover and rarely repeated, so buildings drift into waste. Emissions penalties and code-required acceptance tests raise the stakes, yet commissioning agents are labor-constrained.
solution: Connect through a BACnet or BAS gateway with read/write access. An LLM converts Sequences of Operation (ASHRAE Guideline 36 or project spec PDFs) into bounded test scripts with safety envelopes and automatic rollback. Overnight runs produce pass/fail results with evidence, a deficiency list with estimated savings, and signed test reports for compliance. Re-run quarterly, with operator approval built in.
why_now: BAS gateways and cloud connections are mainstream. LLMs can now parse sequences and generate test logic. Building performance standards, including LL97, are producing real penalties, and utilities pay for measured savings. Commissioning firms cannot hire enough engineers.
revenue_model: $5-15k per building test campaign, $1-3k per month for ongoing quarterly testing, white-label resale through commissioning firms at about 30% margin, and shared-savings deals with ESCOs.
non_obvious_insight: Active probing creates ground-truth labels that passive analytics lack, and the law already requires many of the tests, so automating them cuts a mandatory cost rather than selling a discretionary energy project. Chaos engineering is routine in software but almost unknown in buildings because nobody trusts write access, so the real product is the safety envelope, rollback and operator sign-off, more than the AI.
first_30_days: Partner with two commissioning-authority firms. Agree on five common tests (economizer, VAV minimum flow, chiller staging, sensor cross-checks, pump changeover). Run them on 3 buildings with BACnet access at a fixed fee priced at 40-60% of a manual test, and document the energy findings.

title: Privacy-Compliant Monetization for Faith Apps
one_liner: An audit-plus-replacement stack for small prayer, Quran, Bible, Torah and temple apps whose ad SDKs quietly turn every user into a sale of religious-belief data.
customer: Independent and mid-size publishers of ad-funded faith apps (prayer times, Quran, Bible/devotional, Hindu calendar, Zmanim, halal finders, congregation apps) and church-management/giving software vendors serving thousands of congregations.
problem: Religious beliefs are special-category data under GDPR Art. 9 and 'sensitive data' requiring opt-in consent under nearly every US state privacy law. Maryland's law goes further, banning the sale of sensitive data and limiting collection to what is strictly necessary (in force since Oct 2025, verify enforcement dates). Regulators have treated mere use of a niche app as revealing sensitive traits (Norway's Grindr fine, upheld on appeal, verify). Reporting in 2020 showed a Muslim prayer app's location data reaching a broker and then US military contractors. Yet most small faith apps run stock ad SDKs with device IDs and location, have no consent flow and no counsel. The briefing notes non-Christian faith apps are far less served than Hallow-style Christian ones, and the IAPP says state privacy momentum is at an all-time high.
solution: (1) A public audit tool that scans app binaries and web properties for SDK data flows and issues a scorecard plus a legal-risk memo by state and EU. (2) A drop-in compliance SDK: a consent manager that treats every user as sensitive by default, server-side region logic, data maps and DPIA templates in Arabic, Urdu, Bahasa, Hebrew, Spanish and Portuguese. (3) A contextual, ID-free sponsorship marketplace where halal, kosher, umrah, church-goods and faith-nonprofit sponsors book placements by content context (for example an iftar-times page). (4) A subpoena and data-request playbook with minimal retention by design, so the app has little to hand over.
why_now: State privacy laws with sensitive-data opt-in are now the norm and Maryland's strict rules are enforceable in 2026 (verify dates). GDPR fines total EUR 7.16B with 229 new cases in 2026 (per briefing). Faith apps are booming (Hallow reached #1 in the US App Store) while faith data is politically charged around surveillance and immigration enforcement.
revenue_model: $149-499/month per app for SDK plus audit. 25-30% revenue share on contextual sponsorship. One-time $1.5-3k audit and fix sprint. Enterprise contracts with church-tech vendors.
non_obvious_insight: For a faith app the category itself reveals the belief (the Grindr logic), so 'we do not collect religion' is not a defense. The violation is the ad model, so the fix is a different revenue stream, not a policy PDF. Contextual sponsorship from faith-community advertisers can pay better than junk programmatic. Public scorecards create the sales funnel, because in tight communities reputation and fear move fast.
first_30_days: Audit the top 100 Muslim prayer/Quran apps and 50 Christian, Jewish and Hindu apps with open-source traffic analysis (mitmproxy, Exodus-style trackers). Publish a 'Privacy Scorecard for Faith Apps' and email each publisher. Sell paid fix sprints to 5 pilot apps at about $2k and recruit 5 community sponsors for contextual placements. Team is one privacy lawyer plus one Android engineer.

title: Contingency Collection for Small-Claims Winners
one_liner: Post-judgment enforcement for the $500-$10k creditor who won in court but cannot collect: skip-trace, levy and garnishment paperwork done for a percentage.
customer: Small landlords with unpaid-rent or damage judgments, tenants with deposit judgments, freelancers and contractor-fraud victims, paying a $99 setup plus 25-30% of dollars actually recovered.
problem: Roughly 70-80% of civil and small-claims judgments go uncollected, and the winner must find assets and file every enforcement step alone. Enforcement costs can exceed the judgment, tenants disappear without forwarding addresses, and attorneys skip small cases. Cheap filing tools like trysmallclaims ($149 demand letter, $299 filing) stop at judgment.
solution: Automate post-judgment work: skip-trace the debtor, discover employer and bank via debtor-exam forms, e-file state-specific wage garnishment and bank levy packets, schedule sheriff or constable levies, and calendar renewals and follow-ups. A partner licensed collection agency or attorney in each state handles regulatory compliance. Offer a pre-filing 'collectability score' so creditors learn whether the defendant has a job or bank account before spending on court.
why_now: Self-serve filing tools are creating more small-claims judgments, while enforcement remains manual and state-specific. Consumer data APIs and LLM document drafting make per-state packets cheap, and small landlords face rising unpaid-rent losses and slow evictions, so many are holding judgments they cannot collect.
revenue_model: 25-30% contingency on recovered dollars, $99 setup fee, and a $19 collectability score for pre-filing triage; later B2B seats for landlord associations and property managers.
non_obvious_insight: A widely cited split says about 20% of debtors pay voluntarily, 60% are 'strategic avoiders' who have assets but make the creditor work, and 20% are judgment-proof (https://www.trysmallclaims.com/blog/small-claims-court-judgment-enforcement-tools-by-state). The middle 60% is a repeatable, automatable playbook, and the competitor sells only filing and demand letters. The ABA Journal notes about 80% of civil money judgments remain unenforced and that only 3 of the top 50 law schools teach judgment enforcement (https://www.abajournal.com/voice/article/why-do-80-of-judgments-remain-uncollected). Landlord-side friction is described at https://www.fastevictionservice.com/blog/why-small-claims-court-judgments-are-hard-to-enforce/, which notes costs 'sometimes exceeding the amount of the judgment itself'. Reddit was unreachable, so the r/Landlord and r/legaladvice 'I won, now how do I collect?' pattern is inferred from these secondary sources.
first_30_days: Pick California or Texas. Approach two local apartment or landlord associations and collect 10-20 existing unpaid judgments on contingency. Sign a licensed collection agency or attorney partner, build the skip-trace plus writ and levy templates for one county, run garnishments manually first, and publish recovery statistics after the first 5 collections.

title: On-Demand Human Witnesses for Scrap and Recycled Claims
one_liner: A network of trained, insured, credentialed ex-auditors and QA people who can be dispatched within 24 hours to physically inspect scrap lots and witness recycled-content claims, producing tamper-evident signed reports.
customer: Remote buyers of bales and scrap lots (PET reclaimers, black-mass and tungsten buyers, brokers, traders). Brands making recycled-content claims, and their insurers and lenders. The buyers' own AI purchasing agents consume the reports through an API.
problem: PET bales trade at a record-low 1.44 c/lb while food-grade supply is called constrained, which points to a quality-tier mismatch nobody can see without inspection. Generative AI makes photos, scale tickets and certificates trivially forgeable. Traditional inspectors have minimum fees and multi-day lead times. Mass-balance claims are contested and no standard exists. California's AB 2253 (claim substantiation) was vetoed, leaving brands exposed to litigation. EU rules banning generic green claims (Directive 2024/825) began applying on Sept 27, 2026.
solution: Recruit displaced auditors, QA analysts, supply-chain and compliance staff and give them a one-day protocol course on bale and scrap specs. Dispatch them to open and grade bales, XRF-screen metals, seal loads, witness weigh-outs and attend recycled-content production runs. They use a capture app with device attestation and signed provenance, and every report is machine-readable. Visits cost $95-250 versus $800+ for traditional inspection. Each witness builds a portable, scored reputation, so the credential becomes their asset.
why_now: AI forgery capability is now cheap and widely known, so document trust is falling. The BIS Aug 27 rule adds recordkeeping for black mass and tungsten scrap. Brands need substantiation now that the EU rules apply. Agentic procurement needs verifiable physical inputs. The supply of trained auditors and analysts is growing because of AI-driven cuts.
revenue_model: Per-inspection fee split about 60/40 with the witness. Monthly claim-assurance subscriptions for brands ($1-3K). API and report-verification fees for buyers' agents. Later, a quality-tier index of bales sold to the market.
non_obvious_insight: When AI can fake any document, the scarce commodity is a credentialed human who was physically present. The scrap trade runs on thin margins and unverifiable quality claims, so cheap, fast human presence beats expensive certification. AI displacement supplies the witnesses at the same moment it destroys trust in paperwork.
first_30_days: Pick one corridor with several bale or e-scrap buyers and offer 20 discounted bale inspections to three remote buyers. Recruit and train 10 witnesses (ex-QA and audit). Build the capture flow on existing attestation and C2PA tools. Publish a first bale-quality report from the results.

title: Family Bank: Bank of Mom and Dad, Papered
one_liner: A family office's real job is governance and records, not investing; for $20/mo, give ordinary parents and adult children a promissory-note, autopay and sibling-fairness ledger for the money that already flows between them.
customer: Parents aged 55-75 who lend or give money to adult children (down-payment help, car, tuition, debt payoff, business start), sold as a pair with the adult child (28-45). Elder-law attorneys, mortgage brokers and credit unions are referral channels.
problem: Family lending is handshake-based. Zero-interest loans over $10k invite imputed-interest questions. Gifts above the $19,000 annual exclusion (2026) need Form 709 filings. Medicaid's 60-month look-back treats gifts and forgiven loans as transfers. Mortgage lenders want documented gift letters. Siblings fight at inheritance over who got what because nobody kept records. NAR's 2025 profile shows the median first-time buyer is 40 and 22% received a gift or loan from relatives or friends.
solution: A guided flow decides gift vs loan and generates a note at or above the AFR (August 2026: 4.10% short, 4.35% mid, 4.92% long). ACH autopay collects and pays, and both sides get annual interest statements. A December 'forgiveness engine' forgives up to the exclusion with proper letters. A sibling ledger records every advancement so estates can equalize. Flags fire for Form 709 and Medicaid look-back exposure, and there is a mortgage-ready gift-letter generator plus one-click export to the family's estate attorney. Attorney review is an add-on.
why_now: Median first-time buyer age hit 40 (a record), housing costs push more family help, and long-term-care costs make the Medicaid look-back a live worry for boomer parents. Instant-payment and bank-linking rails make autopay cheap. The 2026 federal estate exemption is $15M, so for most families the value is peace and records, not tax planning.
revenue_model: $20/mo per family (up to 3 active loans); $49 document packs for the free-to-paid funnel; $149 attorney review add-on with referral fees; optional servicing fee; later, a pooled family reserve product.
non_obvious_insight: The killer feature is not the loan, it is the sibling ledger. Most family money fights are about unequal treatment nobody can prove, and family offices solve this with an advancement ledger that ordinary families never get. The loan-vs-gift label is also the pivot point for tax and Medicaid consequences, so classification is the paid moment.
first_30_days: Ship a free AFR calculator and note generator aimed at 'family loan agreement' searches, and sell $49 document packs. Convert 5% to the $20/mo servicing tier. Line up 3 elder-law attorneys who receive leads and review notes. Target 50 paying families.

title: Audit-Proof Family Night in a Box
one_liner: Fixed-price, compliance-packaged family engagement events for Title I schools, paid from the federally required parent-engagement set-aside, with the monitoring binder as the real product.
customer: District Title I coordinators and Title I principals. The money comes from the ESSA parent and family engagement reserve, which is 1 percent of Title I for districts above the size threshold, and most of it must go to schools.
problem: That money is earmarked but scary to spend. Principals fear audit findings over food, childcare, transport, interpreters and incentives, because each has 'necessary and reasonable' tests and must tie back to the district's engagement policy and the school-parent compact. Events get thin turnout of 20 to 30 percent of families. Principals end up buying pizza with sketchy funds, or the money sits unspent until spring.
solution: A fully produced event in a box. It is built around students performing or presenting, and includes a dinner from a local caterer, on-site childcare, ride vouchers, live interpreters and a personal invitation call script. Every event ships with a pre-vetted allowable-cost memo, an agenda tied to the compact and policy, QR sign-in, a parent needs survey, an evaluation report and a monitoring-ready binder generated automatically. Packages are $4.5k to $9k per event, with annual bundles for a district.
why_now: After the July 2025 federal funding freeze scare and post-ESSER budget cuts, coordinators are under pressure to spend every Title I dollar on time and defensibly. Chronic absenteeism has stuck near one in four students, and family engagement is the best-evidenced lever schools have left. States are also stepping up monitoring of federal-funds documentation.
revenue_model: Per-event fixed fee ($4.5k to $9k), annual multi-event contracts ($25k to $60k per school), and a district-wide compliance template license.
non_obvious_insight: Turnout comes from four things nobody bundles: kids on stage, food, childcare in the building, and a personal call from a known adult. The real blocker is not attendance. It is the principal's fear of an audit finding, so the binder is what they are buying and the event is only the delivery vehicle. Vendors that sell 'parent engagement software' miss this because the software cannot make an allowable-cost decision.
first_30_days: Read one state's Title I monitoring protocol and write a two-page allowable-cost memo. Get two Title I coordinators to comment on it and agree to a template. Pitch 5 principals you know, and run 3 pilot events at cost with a local caterer and a bilingual emcee. Capture turnout data versus the school's usual events. Turn the paperwork into a reusable binder generator.

title: Surge Beds: Pre-Contracted Lodging for Catastrophe Responders
one_liner: Sell adjuster firms and storm contractors reserved-bed options on inland RV pads, seasonal parks and closed motels, contracted before landfall at prices that stay legal after an emergency declaration.
customer: Independent-adjuster firms' cat operations and logistics managers, restoration franchisees, roofing and mitigation contractors bringing out-of-state crews, and utility subcontractors. Reservation fees are paid pre-season, activation nights after the event.
problem: After landfall or a big wildfire, responder capacity is limited by beds, not people. Adjusters sleep in cars, 90 minutes away, or in RVs on borrowed lots, and deployed adjusters quit or rotate out. Anti-gouging laws (34 states, typically capping increases at about 10% for 30 days after a declaration) stop hotels from raising rates, so price cannot allocate scarce rooms; they simply sell out to whoever had a relationship or a corporate block.
solution: A lodging-capacity option network. Sign inland owners 60-150 miles from likely landfall zones (seasonal RV parks and park-model communities that sit empty in hurricane season, church halls and school gyms, closed-for-season motels, dorms, and short-term-rental owners willing to accept 30-day minimum stays) to pre-agreed rates that are lawful because they were set before the emergency. Buyers pay a per-bed or per-site reservation fee before the season, credited against activation nights. Add paid extras that responders actually need: Starlink, laundry, catering, portable showers, secure parking for trucks and trailers. Extend to wildfire base camps in CA, OR and CO.
why_now: Quick searches surfaced no dedicated adjuster-lodging option marketplace, only ad hoc use of RV parks after storms like Michael. Two years of quiet U.S. hurricane landfalls (none in 2025, and no hurricane at all in the 2026 Atlantic season through Sept 11) mean firms have not tested surge logistics and will be caught out by the next big one. Adjuster and contractor headcounts are being squeezed by automation and tight margins, so a predictable per-bed cost is more attractive than scrambling. Anti-gouging enforcement has grown more aggressive.
revenue_model: Reservation fees of roughly $400-$900 per bed per season, credited against activation nights. On activation, a 15-20% margin over the pre-agreed owner rate, plus ancillary services (connectivity, meals, laundry) at 30-40% margin. Later, annual enterprise contracts with IA firms for guaranteed headcount blocks.
non_obvious_insight: Because gouging laws freeze price after the declaration, the only legal way to buy certainty is to contract early, which turns lodging into an options market where the option seller (a snowbird RV park empty from June to October) has almost no other use for its inventory in exactly the months responders need it. Insiders know the constraint on a cat deployment is where 200 adjusters sleep, not how many exist.
first_30_days: Call 50 seasonal RV parks, campgrounds and small motel owners across the inland Gulf Coast, Carolinas and Texas and sign non-binding LOIs on rates and bed counts. Draft a one-page option contract reviewed by a hospitality lawyer for gouging-law compliance. Pitch logistics managers at 8 IA firms and restoration franchise groups on 2027 pre-season blocks, aiming for 2-3 signed reservation deposits of 20-50 beds each. Build a simple booking and check-in app with texted access codes and a map of inventory.

title: Compliance-First CDL School Roll-Up for Carriers
one_liner: Buy the clean CDL schools that survived the federal crackdown, run them with AI scheduling and audit-ready records, and get paid per hired graduate by carriers.
customer: Trucking carriers (pay-per-hire or tuition guarantees), students (financed), and workforce boards. School owners are the sellers.
problem: FMCSA removed nearly 3,000 providers from the Training Provider Registry and has thousands more under investigation. The non-domiciled CDL rule effective 16 March 2026 removed an estimated 90,000+ CDLs. Carriers need legitimate, US-domiciled drivers with provable training, and independent schools are mom-and-pop operations with thin documentation, idle trucks and scarce instructors.
solution: Acquire mid-size schools with clean records. AI ops: scheduling that keeps trucks and instructors busy, automatic ELDT and registry records with an audit-ready evidence packet per student, simulators and camera or telematics coaching that shorten range hours, and a placement engine matching graduates to carriers. Carriers pay a bounty per hire and back student financing.
why_now: The 2026 crackdown turned record quality into a scarce, acquirable asset, and capacity is tight. Carriers want vetted sources of drivers, and simulators and telematics are now cheap.
revenue_model: Tuition of $4k to $8k per student (self-pay, financed, or WIOA-funded), carrier placement fees of $3k to $6k per hire, and simulator licensing to smaller schools.
non_obvious_insight: After a regulatory purge, provenance is the product. The school that can prove every training hour becomes a carrier's preferred feeder farm, so audit-ready data is worth more than the trucks. Reputation risk from CDL mills is a barrier to entry for bad actors and a marketing asset for a clean operator.
first_30_days: Sign a letter of intent with one small school owner on seller financing. Sign two regional carriers to a pilot pay-per-hired-graduate agreement. Put cameras and telematics on two training trucks and produce a sample audit packet. Publish pass and placement data.

title: Good-Better-Best Estimate Engine for Vet Clinics
one_liner: AI scribes are turning into a free feature, so the money moves to the moment a client sees the estimate: automate tiered spectrum-of-care plans that turn declines into partial acceptance.
customer: Emergency/urgent-care hospitals and 2-10 DVM independent general practices, where estimates over $1,000 are routine. Buyer is the practice owner or hospital manager.
problem: Per the briefing, 85% of vet professionals say clients decline care at estimates of $1,000 or less, and 86% alter treatment plans weekly for financial reasons. Estimates are still hand-built as one gold-standard plan, so declines are lost revenue and a source of moral distress (33% of vets find below-gold care distressing). Nobody logs why clients decline.
solution: Reads the diagnosis or SOAP note from any scribe or PIMS and drafts three clinician-approved tiers: full workup, stabilize-and-monitor, and essential/palliative. Each tier is priced from the clinic's own fee schedule, with consent language, expected-outcome ranges and stage-gated steps (approve step 1 now, decide step 2 after results). Financing and insurance pre-check sit on the same screen. Every decline reason is captured and feeds a protocol library written with boarded clinicians. Ships as a browser overlay on the PIMS estimate screen.
why_now: IDEXX bought the CoVet AI scribe on 2026-09-16 and says it will stay compatible with non-IDEXX systems. That marks documentation AI as a bundled strategic feature and squeezes standalone scribes. Clinic visits have reportedly fallen three years running, and price, not demand, is the constraint.
revenue_model: SaaS at $300-600 per clinic per month, plus an optional success fee of 3-5% of incremental accepted revenue measured against a pre-pilot baseline. Later, anonymized decline-reason data sold to insurers and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders think the AI prize is saving doctors' time on notes. The budget line is revenue at the decision moment, and the scribe is just a commodity input to it. The decline reason is a dataset nobody collects, and it is what financiers and insurers most want.
first_30_days: Sign 5 ER/urgent-care sites and 5 independents. Take each site's last 20 de-identified declined estimates, have a contract boarded vet rebuild them as three-tier plans, and run a 4-week pilot tracking acceptance rate. Charge a $1,500 pilot fee. Prototype the browser overlay with an LLM plus the clinic's fee-schedule export.

title: Digital Journeyman: Ride-Along Capture for Apprentices
one_liner: Retiring tradespeople wear chest cameras for a few job days, and AI turns the footage into a code-aware 'digital master' that also verifies apprentices' on-the-job hours and technique.
customer: Electrical, plumbing and HVAC contractors and apprenticeship sponsors (JATCs, IEC and ABC chapters), community-college trade programs; retiring journeymen are paid royalty recipients.
problem: Trade apprenticeships take 4-5 years and are bottlenecked by scarce journeyman mentors, many retiring, while the sponsor bottleneck is supervision. OJT hours are logged by hand and cannot be verified, and mentoring quality is inconsistent. The entry path for electricians has about 72.7k openings a year.
solution: V1: apprentice phone or chest-cam capture that produces AI-verified OJT hour logs by task type for sponsor reporting. V2: an 'ask the master' agent trained on captured ride-alongs plus the locally adopted code edition, with escalation to a live mentor. V3: form-check feedback on tasks like conduit bending and terminations. Retiring journeymen earn per-use royalties.
why_now: Video-understanding models can now parse hours of messy jobsite footage, camera-equipped smart glasses reached consumers in late 2025, and data-center demand is stretching journeymen thin. Apprenticeship policy support is growing.
revenue_model: $30-60 per apprentice per month paid by sponsors or contractors, capture-project fees for retiring-mentor programs, and licensing of the annotated video library to trade schools.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input in the trades is not information but supervised repetition. Verified hours and over-the-shoulder feedback multiply each journeyman's supervisory capacity, and retiring masters' tacit knowledge is a wasting asset worth capturing in the next two years.
first_30_days: Partner with one IEC or ABC chapter or contractor. Equip 10 apprentices with $60 chest-mount phone rigs. Pay 3 retiring journeymen to record about 40 job-hours. Deliver an OJT hour-log report a sponsor accepts and charge $40 per apprentice per month. Handle site-owner consent up front.

title: Monetization Compliance-as-Code for Free-to-Play Studios
one_liner: A linter that reads a studio's store and gacha configuration and flags per-country, per-age-band violations, with an auditable rulebook curated by counsel.
customer: Mid-size free-to-play mobile and PC studios and publishers (10-300 staff) selling in the EU, UK, Brazil, Australia and US states.
problem: Rules diverge fast. Brazil's 2025 child-protection law restricts loot boxes for minors (in force in 2026), the EU consumer authorities set 2025 principles on virtual currency pricing, and an EU Digital Fairness Act proposal is expected around late 2026. Roblox age tiers and Discord age checks add age-band segmentation. Studios rely on $400-600 per hour legal memos and hand-checked spreadsheets.
solution: Ingest offer tables, gacha odds, currency bundles and subscription flows from LiveOps exports or APIs. Flag violations per market and age band against a versioned rulebook, produce audit-ready evidence, and gate builds in CI.
why_now: Brazil's restrictions took effect in 2026, the Digital Fairness Act is in the pipeline, and platform age tiers force age-aware storefronts. Enforcement history (Epic's FTC settlements) shows the cost of missing this.
revenue_model: $500-3,000 per month per title, $5-15k onboarding, and a premium tier with counsel-reviewed rule updates.
non_obvious_insight: Games compliance is sold as legal advice, but violations live in JSON: drop tables, prices, labels and flows. That is machine-checkable, law firms sell memos, and nobody ships a linter.
first_30_days: Have a games-regulatory lawyer co-write a 4-market rulebook. Build a linter for one config format (Remote Config plus a gacha CSV). Offer free audits to 10 mobile studios and convert 2 to $1k per month.

title: Data Act Broker for Equipment Owners
one_liner: File and operationalize EU Data Act data-access demands so independent service shops can finally read the diagnostics that elevator, heat-pump, forklift and tractor makers lock away.
customer: Independent maintenance and service companies in the EU (starting with elevator/escalator maintainers, then commercial heat-pump installers, forklift and ag-machinery shops). They pay per monitored asset per month. Equipment-owning businesses (building managers, hospitals, logistics sites) are the secondary payer, because they hold the legal right.
problem: Original manufacturers use exclusive access to machine diagnostics and fault logs to keep 60-80% of the lucrative service market. Independents work blind, so they lose contracts to OEMs. The EU Data Act (applicable since 12 Sep 2025) gives the user of a connected product, including a business, the right to get the data the product generates. The user can also have it handed to any third party of their choice. In practice almost nobody exercises the right. The paperwork is unfamiliar, OEMs stall, and the data arrives in a different format from every vendor.
solution: An agency-plus-plumbing service. (1) Sign a user-authorization letter with the equipment owner. (2) Auto-generate and file the Article 4/5 access and third-party-sharing requests to each OEM and track statutory response deadlines. (3) Ingest whatever comes back, whether an API, a file dump or a portal export. (4) Normalize it into one cross-vendor schema per asset class. (5) Give the independent shop a fleet-health dashboard and fault-prediction alerts. Add a public compliance scorecard showing which OEMs comply, and escalate the ones that do not to national enforcement authorities.
why_now: The Data Act became applicable on 12 Sep 2025. On 12 Sep 2026, 16 days ago, its design obligation started applying to newly placed connected products, so data must be accessible by default. The right-to-repair movement is at peak momentum. OEM stonewalling now generates complaints that regulators must act on. No one has industrialized user-side requests yet, so the first mover sets the standard schema and templates.
revenue_model: Setup fee of about 50-150 EUR per asset for the request and integration work, plus 4-12 EUR per asset per month for the normalized feed and health analytics. Add-ons: predictive-maintenance alerts and a white-label owner portal. Later: sell anonymized cross-fleet reliability benchmarks to insurers and asset owners.
non_obvious_insight: A legal right is worthless until someone industrializes exercising it. The Data Act gives the data-access key to the owner, not the repairer, so the winning business acts as the owner's agent and sells the result to the repairer. The moat is accumulated request templates, OEM-by-OEM response knowledge, and one normalized schema. Every OEM refusal also becomes evidence for regulators, which turns compliance friction into marketing.
first_30_days: Pick one vertical and one country pair, for example independent elevator maintainers in Germany and the Netherlands, and reach them through trade associations. Retain a Data Act lawyer for a fixed fee to finalize request templates. Recruit 5 independent shops, get user-authorization letters covering about 50 units, and file the requests. Log every OEM response and format. Charge a pilot fee of about 1-2k EUR per shop for delivered data plus a first fleet report. Publish an OEM response-time tracker to build inbound demand. Expect uneven enforcement, so keep the pilot to OEMs that respond and use the ones that stonewall as regulator evidence.

title: Zero-Commission Motor Third-Party Renewal Rails
one_liner: If motor third-party pays agents 0%, nobody sells the mandatory cover, so insurers need a cost-plus renewal utility.
customer: Indian general insurers, especially public-sector ones, and fleet owners; insurers pay a per-renewal fee.
problem: The IRDAI draft (Sep 23) cuts commission caps from 30% to 20%, sets 0% on motor third-party and 5% on own-damage. PB Fintech fell 36% in a day, and agents and aggregators lose any reason to chase mandatory renewals.
solution: Automated renewal reminders using expiry data from dealers and registration records, sent as WhatsApp messages in local languages with UPI payment. Charge a flat servicing fee. The wedge is two-wheeler third-party renewals in one state for one insurer.
why_now: The draft is out for comment now, and insurers must find distribution that costs less than commission.
revenue_model: Rs 30-80 per renewal from the insurer, with own-damage upsell.
non_obvious_insight: When distribution stops paying, a mandatory product needs a utility rather than a marketplace, and the underwriter is the natural buyer. The draft could change, so build for both outcomes.
first_30_days: Pitch three insurers. Run a 5,000-vehicle renewal test using expiry lists from a dealer network.

title: Buyout Bridge for Flood-Prone Counties
one_liner: Run the paperwork of county flood buyouts and front cash to owners, reimbursed when grants land.
customer: County and municipal floodplain managers and state hazard-mitigation offices, paying from program administration budgets. Later, impact and philanthropic capital for the bridge fund.
problem: Risk Rating 2.0 pushes premiums toward full risk (median $689 versus about $1,288 needed, per CRS, secondary source), eroding equity in repeatedly flooded homes. Owners want out, but FEMA programs are erratic: BRIC was cancelled in April 2025, restored by court order and reinstated Mar 18 2026, with applications closed July 23 2026. Buyouts take years, so owners sit in limbo or sell at fire-sale prices.
solution: An operations and software backbone for county acquisition programs: eligibility, duplication-of-benefits tracking, appraisal, title, relocation counseling, demolition procurement, open-space deed restrictions and reimbursement compliance. Then add a pooled bridge fund that pays owners in 60-90 days and is repaid from grants.
why_now: The NFIP glide path to full-risk pricing, plus the BRIC cancel-and-restore whiplash, leaves states building their own programs.
revenue_model: $3-8K fixed admin fee per acquisition, and later a bridge-loan spread.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck is not money but cash timing and paperwork, and governments will pay for throughput more readily than for software.
first_30_days: Pick 3 counties with repetitive-loss acquisition backlogs and offer to run 20 properties under a $25K pilot. Publish time-to-close as the benchmark.

title: Slop-Rating Feed for Kids' Filters
one_liner: A channel- and app-level data feed that classifies children's content as verified human-made, AI slop or unknown, sold to school web filters and kids' hardware.
customer: School-district web-filter and parental-control vendors, kids' tablet, audio-player and smart-speaker makers, and school districts directly.
problem: Fairplay found that 104 of the first 500 videos recommended to a fresh account were AI slop. On 1 Apr 2026 more than 200 organisations, including the American Federation of Teachers, asked YouTube to label and ban AI content on kids' surfaces, and YouTube said only that it is developing labels. Filters classify by topic (violence, adult), not by how content was produced.
solution: Continuously crawl kids-targeted channels, apps, audiobooks and games. Classify provenance using channel behaviour, voice and image-model signals, upload cadence and template reuse, plus human review. Add a 'verified human-made' tier through creator attestations and audits. Deliver category lists by API keyed on channel ID, domain or app package, plus teacher whitelist packs.
why_now: Spring 2026 investigations (NYT, Fairplay, CBC) and the April coalition letter made AI slop a school and parent issue. The EU AI Act's Article 50 labelling is beginning, and 1:1 school device fleets need a new filter category now.
revenue_model: $20-200k per year data licences to filter vendors, $0.10-0.50 per-device royalties from hardware makers, and $1-3 per student per year for districts.
non_obvious_insight: A platform's own AI label will always be optional and gameable. The buyer is whoever sits between the child and the platform, and they already buy category feeds. Selling a new dimension (provenance) into an existing distribution channel avoids consumer acquisition entirely.
first_30_days: Build a 20k-channel labelled seed set with three teacher or parent reviewers. Ship a free 'slop score' browser extension for teachers to collect signals and leads. Pitch three mid-size filter and parental-control vendors with a sample feed.

title: Substitute-Plan Binders for Retiring Business Owners
one_liner: Retired teachers interview 60+ owner-operators and write a 'sub plan' any stranger could use to run the shop for a week, sold through business brokers.
customer: Owner-operators aged 60+ of $300k-$3M revenue businesses that depend on the owner's head (HVAC and plumbing, vet and dental practices, hardware stores, salons, daycares, landscaping). The channel and co-payer is the business broker, plus SBA lenders, CPAs and estate attorneys. Acquirers such as search-fund and ETA buyers pay later for a 'day-one' version.
problem: About 40% of small business owners are boomers, and roughly 6 million businesses will change hands by 2035. Around 70% of listed small businesses never sell, and about half of owners have no succession plan. Buyers and lenders can't underwrite what lives only in the owner's memory. Owners refuse to write SOPs, but they will talk for hours. Brokers watch listings die at the diligence stage because 'the business is the owner.'
solution: Two half-day interview sessions plus a video walk-through of the shop. Teachers are trained to draw knowledge out of people with questions. The output is a 20-40 page Sub Plan written in the classroom genre. It covers the daily schedule and routines, where the keys and passwords are, the 'kids to watch' (the difficult customer, the vendor who needs a call before noon, the employee who needs praise), emergency procedures, a first-hour and first-week script, and 'what NOT to do.' The org chart is drawn as a seating chart showing who actually influences whom. Then comes the sub test. A stranger runs a 4-hour shift from the binder, and every gap they hit gets fixed. The result becomes a diligence exhibit in the sale memorandum. AI transcription and structuring keep labor cost low, and the human elicitation stays the scarce part.
why_now: Coverage of the 'Great Ownership Transfer' peaked in 2026 (McKinsey, Forbes and others). First-time buyers via SBA 7(a) loans and search funds are flooding the market and underwriting transferability. AI transcription and structuring dropped the cost of capturing tacit knowledge by roughly 10x in the last two years. The oldest boomers turn 80 this year, and estate attorneys are seeing more 'owner died, business worthless in 90 days' cases.
revenue_model: $2,400 flat per binder, usually rolled into the broker's listing package. Brokers get a referral credit of about $300. There is a $49/month 'living binder' update plan. Buyers can pay $1,500 for a post-close rewrite. There is a $600 add-on for estate attorneys covering an 'if I'm hit by a bus' version.
non_obvious_insight: The sub plan is the most battle-tested knowledge-transfer document in existence. Every teacher has written hundreds of them for a stranger with 30 unpredictable kids and six hours. No consultant has that reps count. The real asset in a small business is the informal 'kids to watch' list, which never appears in any SOP. Sellers don't fail because they lack documents. They fail because nobody asked the right questions in the right order.
first_30_days: Recruit 4-5 retired teachers who like interviewing. Pick one metro and pitch 20 business brokers with one offer: 'give me your stalest listing, the one that has sat 9+ months, and I'll run a free pilot binder.' Do 3 free pilots in exchange for testimonials and an intro to the broker's next 5 listings. Then charge $2,400. Add SCORE chapters, SBDCs and estate attorneys as second-wave channels.

title: Solar Defection Radar for African Utilities
one_liner: Africa's invisible solar and battery boom leaves utilities, banks and insurers blind, so measure it district by district.
customer: African distribution utilities and regulators, development finance institutions, commercial banks and insurers.
problem: Africa installs 17 GW in 2026 (+45%), 75% of it distributed. Ember's estimates are 2x official figures, and only 14 of 54 countries reported 2025 data. Utilities cannot see which paying customers are leaving, and lenders cannot price the assets.
solution: Estimate installed solar and battery stock per district from customs and import data, rooftop detection in satellite imagery and installer sales data. The wedge is a quarterly district-level report for Nigeria or Kenya, sold to one utility and one DFI.
why_now: Chinese exports hit records and batteries now outsell panels in import dollars. Ember's 'invisible boom' finding is public but nobody has productised it.
revenue_model: $25-100k per year per institution, plus bespoke studies for DFIs.
non_obvious_insight: When self-generation outruns official statistics, the first credible dataset becomes the reference for tariffs, credit and insurance pricing.
first_30_days: Combine public Chinese export data, Ember figures and roof imagery for Lagos and Kano. Give a free sample to three utilities and one DFI.

title: AI Kill-Switch Drills That Unlock Affirmative Cover
one_liner: A third-party 'shutdown drill' and evidence certificate proving a company can halt its AI systems fast, so carriers will write affirmative AI cover and insureds can qualify for it.
customer: Mid-market companies (50-2,000 staff) running customer-facing or agentic AI, paying $4-12k per year. Their cyber and E&O brokers and MGAs are secondary payers, at a per-verified-insured fee.
problem: Admitted carriers are adding AI exclusions to general liability and E&O while specialty carriers sell narrow affirmative AI add-ons. Buyers cannot show underwriters that they can stop a misbehaving AI system, so they either go uncovered or pay E&S prices.
solution: A quarterly 'AI shutdown drill'. We inventory the client's AI systems and agents, run a timed kill-switch and rollback test with a runbook, and log the evidence. We issue a carrier-readable attestation, modeled on how MFA and EDR scans became underwriting inputs, with the API and PDF formats brokers can attach to submissions. Carriers and MGAs get standardized control data for pricing AI endorsements.
why_now: Beazley announced an 'industry-first' AI Voluntary Shutdown endorsement on 2026-09-25. CFC is embedding affirmative AI wording across its portfolio (2026-09-24). Insurers are debating targeted exclusions for systemic AI events and for autonomous decisions made 'as designed' (2026-08-31). Affirmative AI cover is only now shipping, and its triggers depend on shutdown capability nobody yet verifies.
revenue_model: Annual drill subscription of $4-12k per insured. Per-attestation fees of $250-500 paid by MGAs and carriers, or a revenue share on AI endorsements that bind with a certificate attached. A later data licence to carriers.
non_obvious_insight: Demand is visible in insurer behavior. Surplus lines coverage is described as filling in where admitted carriers are 'implementing the best, most absolute AI exclusions and limiting coverage in traditional general liability policies' (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/09/23/886403.htm). Beazley's new AI Voluntary Shutdown and AI Regulatory Defence endorsements pay to suspend a malfunctioning AI system (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/09/25/886788.htm). Travelers' risk index finds 89% of businesses use AI daily but only 59% have employee AI-use practices, so a verification gap exists (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/09/23/886527.htm). Insurers are discussing exclusions for AI models causing correlated losses and for agents acting autonomously (https://www.insurancejournal.com/news/national/2026/08/31/883343.htm). Cyber insurance took off once controls became verifiable and discountable, and the same will happen for AI. The scarce asset is neutral proof of a control, not another AI policy-analysis tool.
first_30_days: Write a one-page shutdown-drill standard covering agents, model-vendor kill paths, rollback and comms. Recruit 3 cyber brokers to nominate 10 pilot clients. Run 5 free drills to build case studies, then approach 2 MGAs or carriers already selling affirmative AI cover (CFC and Beazley are the visible ones) with the sample attestation. Charge from drill number 6 and close the first 3 paying clients through broker channels.

title: Real-Time Dental Benefits Texting Before December 31
one_liner: A dental-office tool that texts patients their actual remaining insurance dollars and a wallet card, filling the Q4 schedule that insurers' broken apps leave empty.
customer: Independent dental practices with 1-5 dentists, first those on Open Dental (open API) or Dentrix. The owner-dentist or office manager pays.
problem: Patients cannot find what benefit they have left. The insurers' own apps are among the worst-rated apps in the category. The Delta Dental Mobile App averages 1.49 stars over 1,809 ratings and United Concordia averages 2.48. Reviews describe 40+ login failures and complaints such as 'Doesn't let you see your EOB', 'Doesn't even show claims payments', 'App displays the wrong Member ID number' and 'Claims on app don't match claims on web'. Most benefit years reset on December 31, so treatment plans go unscheduled while the practice's front desk spends hours on the phone. Practice campaigns rely on benefit data stored in the practice software, which goes stale.
solution: Each night the tool runs real-time eligibility checks (X12 270/271 through an existing dental clearinghouse) for patients with accepted but unscheduled treatment. It calculates remaining annual maximum and deductible met. It then sends a personalized text with the patient's actual figure and a booking link, for example: 'You have $1,120 of your Delta Dental benefit left, and it expires Dec 31.' It also issues an Apple or Google Wallet pass with the insurance card and remaining balance. The front desk gets a ranked call list with expected production. There is no generative AI involved, and it works from live payer data, not from what the practice software last stored.
why_now: Today is Sept 28, 2026, so the Q4 use-it-or-lose-it window is open now and a pilot can run Oct 15 to Dec 20. Insurer apps still bounce users to a web browser to log in and show little data. Practice-software APIs and clearinghouse eligibility APIs are available to small vendors. A tool that ships in October can be measured in booked production before year end.
revenue_model: A free Q4 pilot with a 5% success fee on collected production from attributed appointments. After the pilot, $299/month flat per practice, or $199/month plus 3% of attributed production. Later add-ons: a January 'new benefits' campaign and a mid-year campaign for plans with fiscal-year resets.
non_obvious_insight: The insight is that the insurer's app is so bad that the dental office is the only interface patients trust, and the office has never been given real-time dollar figures in one place. The evidence is patient-side, not practice-side, so the practice-side demand (fuller Q4 schedules) still needs to be proven in the pilot. Evidence: Delta Dental Mobile App (1.49 stars, 1,809 ratings; 'Doesn't let you see your EOB'; login failures) at https://apps.apple.com/us/app/id1585628503 and its review feed at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=1585628503/sortby=mostrecent/xml. United Concordia Dental (2.48 stars; 'Doesn't recognize my member id'; EOB PDFs fail to load; no Apple Wallet ID) at https://itunes.apple.com/us/rss/customerreviews/id=522392221/sortby=mostrecent/xml. Practice-side friction: Dentrix reviewers cite 20+ hours on phone support during a forced migration at https://www.softwareadvice.com/dental/dentrix-profile/reviews/. The wedge sits beside the practice-management system, so the practice does not have to replace it.
first_30_days: Days 1-10: integrate the Open Dental API and one clearinghouse's eligibility API, and run the calculation on a test practice. Days 10-20: recruit 5 practices through Open Dental user forums and dentist Facebook groups, offering a free pilot with success-fee terms. Days 20-30: launch the first campaigns, tracking texts sent, appointments booked and production. Turn the results into a case study to sell more practices before mid-November and for next year's Q4.
